title: Basic Head-to-Toe Assessment Concepts

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think about washing a car. If you scrub wherever your eye lands, you will eventually leave a door or a wheel untouched and never notice. If you always start at the roof and work down to the tires, you finish in the same order every time and nothing gets skipped. Cephalocaudal is that rule applied to a body: head first, feet last, same path every time. The payoff is not speed, it is that a missed step becomes obvious.

### Question 2

Picture figuring out a wrapped present. You look at it, then squeeze it, then thump it to hear whether it is hollow, then hold it to your ear. If you squeezed and thumped first, you would have already dented the paper and changed what you were trying to observe. Bodies work the same way: each technique disturbs the thing the next one measures, so you order them from gentlest to most disruptive.

### Question 3

If a friend says the soup is too spicy, you cannot check that claim, because the tasting happens inside them. If you put a thermometer in the soup and it reads 180 degrees, anyone in the room can look at the same dial. The tricky part is that subjective things can still come with numbers. A pain score of 6 is still the patient reporting what only they can feel; it just wears a number as a disguise.

### Question 4

Bowel sounds are the gut moving on its own schedule. Thumping and pressing on the belly is a nudge that can make it speed up or go quiet, so whatever you hear after that is partly your own doing rather than the patient's baseline. Listening first is how you get the gut's honest rhythm. That single fact is why the belly is the one region where the listening step jumps the line.

### Question 5

When you walk into an unfamiliar room, you register things before you read a single label: whether it is tidy, whether a window is cracked, whether the air smells wrong. That first sweep decides where you look closer. The general survey is that sweep aimed at a person, and it is doing real work, because a patient who cannot finish a sentence or cannot stand up has already told you which part of the exam matters most.

### Question 6

A comprehensive assessment is the full inspection before you buy a house: every room, every pipe, so you learn what normal looks like for that particular house. A focused assessment is what happens when the kitchen faucet starts dripping three months later: you check the sink, not the roof. The order matters. Without the full inspection on file, you have no way to know whether the drip is new.

### Question 7

One sock that looks a bit stretched out is hard to judge on its own, because you do not remember how it started. Hold it next to its match and the difference is instantly obvious. Bodies come in matched pairs for the same convenience: the fastest way to spot something off in one calf is the other calf. Notice the limit, though. Comparison tells you the two differ, not which one is the problem, so you still examine both.

### Question 8

Read the categories as a staircase where a reading lands on the highest step either number reaches. Normal needs both numbers low. Elevated is a narrow step that only exists when the top number has risen to 120 to 129 while the bottom number is still under 80, so a diastolic of 86 disqualifies it immediately. Here 134 sits in the 130 to 139 band and 86 sits in the 80 to 89 band, and both bands name the same step: stage 1.

### Question 9

The moment someone mentions your breathing, you start steering it. That is the whole problem in one sentence. Breathing is the only vital sign with a manual override, which is why you cannot talk your pulse into slowing down but you can absolutely talk your breathing into it. So the examiner keeps a hand on your wrist as if still counting your pulse and quietly counts your chest instead, because the number worth having is the one your body chooses when nobody appears to be watching.

### Question 10

Each technique can only answer its own kind of question. Looking answers shape and color. Tapping answers whether what is underneath is air or something solid. Listening answers whether things are moving. None of those can tell you whether the tissue gives way under a steady press, and that is exactly what "soft" means. Pressing is palpation, so that phrase could not have come from anywhere else, and the word nontender simply says the patient did not hurt while the examiner pressed.

### Question 11

Imagine a lab notebook whose only entry is "the experiment worked." No measurements, no observations, nothing anyone can check or repeat. That is exactly what "patient is anxious" leaves behind. Write what you actually saw and heard, such as pacing, a shaky voice, and "I can't stop worrying," and two things become possible that were not before: a colleague can decide whether they agree with you, and tomorrow's nurse can tell whether the patient is better or worse.

### Question 12

Think in layers. State law is the speed limit, and no employer can give you permission to exceed it. Professional standards are what a competent driver does regardless of posted signs, like checking mirrors, and they are what a court points to when asking whether you drove reasonably. Facility policy is the rule for one parking garage, five miles per hour on the ramp. Ethics is why you care about not hitting anyone. A garage can set its rule stricter than the speed limit; it can never hand you permission to break it.
